transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-11
Time: 10:00 AM UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Jordan Park (CSM), Carlos Vega (Meridian Head of ML), Maya Desai (Engineering Manager), Liam O'Connor (Infra), Nina Park (Product)

Summary: Quick review of pilot cost/unit economics — measured tokens/sec/$, caching savings and how batching impacts latency vs throughput. Align next steps for production pilot scaling and infra constraints.
Topics: 1) benchmark results and metric definitions; 2) caching hit rates and expected savings; 3) batching tradeoffs (p50/p95 latency vs tokens/sec); 4) infra/VPC/egress considerations; 5) pilot next steps.

[00:00] Alex: all right uh thanks everyone for joining, we wanted to walk through the latest numbers from the bench runs we did last week and make sure we're aligned on the cost per unit and what tuning we should do next, mm-hmm.

[00:22] Carlos: yep thanks Alex, real quick — high level i'm mainly focused on what tokens per dollar looks like when we go from our current hosted setup to a dedicated footprint, because ops wants predictable spend.

[00:35] Priya: cool, i'll start with the metric definitions just so we're all using the same math. tokens/sec/$ in our sheet is computed as measured steady-state token throughput divided by hourly cost converted to a per-second-dollar; it's basically how many tokens of generation you can expect for every USD, so higher is better. We also report effective saved tokens from prefix/KV caching as a percent reduction in compute tokens.

[00:58] Maya: quick q — are you normalizing for prompt+response tokens or just response tokens?

[01:05] Priya: good question — we report both, but the primary tokens/sec/$ number in the summary is response-only; in the detail sheet we have combined prompt+response. The pilot traffic is ~60% response-heavy so response-only is a reasonable proxy.

[01:25] Alex: ok so slide, uh i mean sheet highlights — for the representative 512-token use case we ran three configs: hosted (our managed API), dedicated reserved A100s (quantized 4-bit), and dedicated with caching enabled plus batching tuned. The headline: hosted came in at ~3.4k tokens/sec/$, dedicated baseline at ~7.8k tokens/sec/$, and dedicated+cache+batch at ~22.1k tokens/sec/$. Those are rough but representative.

[01:58] Carlos: wait 22k? that is — can you unpack that a bit, what assumptions underlie the 22k number?

[02:05] Priya: yeah the 22.1k reflects a couple of multiplies: quantization reduces per-token compute ~1.9x vs fp16 for this model, batching (avg batch size ~8) nets ~1.5x throughput improvement, and KV cache with a 48% hit rate reduces effective generated tokens by ~2.9x on prefix-heavy flows. Combine those and you get the ~2.8–3x improvement over dedicated baseline; and dedicated already had ~2.3x improvement vs hosted thanks to hardware selection and kernel optimizations.

[02:44] Liam: a quick interjection about cost basis — are you including reserved capacity amortization and support premium in the dedicated rate?

[02:52] Alex: yes — we used our reserved capacity pricing for Dedicated with a 12‑month commit; the hourly cost includes infra + Redwood Dedicated control plane fee (we flagged clearly in the sheet). For hosted we used our pay-as-you-go hosted per-token numbers.

[03:10] Maya: the 48% KV hit rate — is that from our live traces or from the pilot sample?

[03:16] Priya: that's from the pilot synthetic traces we replayed against the model plus a small sample of your production logs you shared last week, Carlos. You did note the sample is biased towards marketing content with lots of reused prefixes which raises the hit-rate a bit vs a pure chat workload.

[03:34] Carlos: right, i think production will be variable — some flows (checkout assistance) have low prefix reuse, others (product copy generation) have high reuse. We're going to run a trace split to see weighted impact.

[03:45] Jordan: (brief) and we put the raw bench runs into the drive, link is in the CRM — Alex will share again.

[03:55] Alex: yep — drive: https://drive.google.com/meridian-redwood-benchmarks (shared). Please note each tab has the raw logs and the calc.

[04:05] [05:00] Priya: on latency tradeoffs — with batch size 1 our p50 per-request generation latency was ~85ms and p95 ~420ms for the 512-token case on dedicated fp16. Increasing batch size to 8 pushed p50 down slightly (due to better GPU utilization) to ~65ms average per token but p95 increased to ~650ms because large batches sometimes queue. That's the usual throughput vs tail-latency tradeoff.

[05:36] Maya: for customer-facing conversational UX we have a p95 requirement of <350ms end-to-end for the fastest routes — do you think we can keep that with batching?

[05:45] Priya: yes for latency-sensitive routes we recommend small batches (1–2) and enable KV caching: with a high KV hit rate the effective compute is much lower, so p95 stays under 350ms. For non-latency-critical bulk generation we use larger batch sizes to improve cost efficiency.

[06:05] Liam: how does cold start affect the economics — if we scale up new pods on dedicated, is there a big penalty?

[06:12] Alex: cold-starts are small for warm pools; for dedicated we keep a minimum pool so cold starts only hit during major spikes. For private/on-prem it's more pronounced — Priya has notes on warm pool sizing.

[06:25] Priya: yep, warm pool sizing recommended: keep 10% headroom for steady-state with autoscale buffers; that adds ~6–8% to the effective hourly cost but reduces cold-start tail. We include that in the Dedicated calc.

[06:45] Carlos: a bit of a finance question — do you have a simple per-route example? Like if checkout has 10M monthly tokens and marketing copy has 50M tokens, what's our blended tokens/sec/$ improvement?

[06:58] Alex: good ask — in the sheet we have a route-by-route calc. Quick summary: checkout heavy route (low cache) sees ~2.1x cost improvement moving to dedicated quantized from hosted; marketing route (heavy cache) sees ~6.4x improvement. Blended across your expected traffic mix we get ~3.6x improvement in tokens per dollar.

[07:25] Nina: any hidden costs we should worry about — egress, S3 charges for logs, or KMS?

[07:33] Liam: egress is real — if we route through a cross-region VPC peer you'll see cloud egress. We need to estimate egress for high-volume routes; i assume the sheet didn't bake heavy cross-region egress?

[07:43] Alex: correct, the primary workbook assumes same-region traffic; we have a separate egress sheet. We'll flag expected incremental egress for the pilot and run scenarios if you share region mappings.

[07:57] Carlos: security/compliance — we need to confirm audit log retention and KMS integration details before escalation, is that on your side?

[08:05] Jordan: yes — we will attach SOC2 docs, KMS integration notes, and the audit-log retention options. Alex will send the security pack after the call.

[08:15] Priya: also one thing on token counting — some clients forget that prompt tokens still count against compute for billing; if you plan heavy prompt-side context we should re-run the cost calc with combined prompt+response.

[08:28] Maya: noted, we'll double-check our prompt sizes.

[08:32] Alex: quick note on quantization quality — we saw no meaningful regression on your eval prompts at 4-bit quant (we ran the Redwood eval harness), but we'll run the targeted regression test against your 50 example prompts to be safe.

[08:45] Carlos: please do, we can't accept LOS regressions.

[08:50] Priya: for rollout strategy we recommend: 1) baseline hosted for non-critical routes; 2) dedicated with cache for high-volume marketing routes; 3) canary dedicated for checkout routes with small batches and strict latency SLOs. We can provide a canary playbook.

[09:06] Nina: timeline ask — if we decide to move to dedicated, how long to provision and tune?

[09:12] Alex: typical provisioning is 2–3 weeks for Dedicated capacity (assuming no special network approvals), plus 1–2 weeks tuning and canary. So about 4–5 weeks from commit to stable canary.

[09:23] Maya: that aligns with our holiday roadmap, so good to know.

[09:28] Liam: one more ops question — what observability do we get? Token-level cost breakouts? Tracing?

[09:34] Priya: yes, Redwood Console exposes per-route token counts, per-token cost, p50/p95 latency, and tracing hooks. We can increase retention as an add‑on. We'll include sample screenshots in the security + ops pack.

[09:46] Carlos: sounds good. i'd like to run the weighted trace split and get back with the expected hit-rate across three route buckets; after that we can re-run the blended cost model.

[09:55] Alex: perfect — recap then...

[10:00] Alex: Recap: 1) Redwood to send the updated benchmark spreadsheet and cost calc (Alex) — link + notes; 2) Priya to run two extra bench runs w/ 80/512 tokens and share numbers; 3) Carlos to share anonymized traces split by route to validate KV hit assumptions; 4) schedule infra deep-dive to confirm VPC/egress implications; 5) Redwood to attach security and KMS/KV cache docs.

[10:20] Maya: thanks everyone — looks like we're moving toward a dedicated pilot for marketing routes and a canary for checkout, pending trace validation.

[10:28] Alex: okay we'll get that out today/tomorrow. Thanks all.

[10:33] Meeting end.

Notes: transcription includes occasional misheard tech terms ("KV cash" instead of "KV cache" in auto-transcript), some speaker labels may be fuzzy. Bench spreadsheet and cost model are the authoritative source for numbers — link provided above.
